questions.stem: A 42 year old man has a 10 hour history of severe headache, fever and vomiting. Bright lights hurt his eyes. His temperature is 39.3°C, pulse rate 118 bpm, BP 108/68 mmHg and GCS 15/15. With his hip flexed, extending his knee causes pain in his back. There is no rash.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Headache, fever, photophobia, vomiting and a positive Kernig's sign in a rapidly progressing severe illness is bacterial meningitis, a medical emergency.

steps.x: Fever, photophobia and a positive Kernig's sign in a severely unwell man.

elim: Does not cause high fever and meningism.
Sudden thunderclap onset, not a febrile illness over hours.
Milder illness; this rapid, severe febrile course is a bacterial emergency.

steps.x: A: Bacterial meningitis. Fever + headache + photophobia + Kernig's = meningitis; severe and fast = bacterial.

questions.stem: A 23 year old woman has 1 day of fever, headache and photophobia. Her temperature is 38.8°C and GCS 15/15. When the doctor passively flexes her neck while she lies flat, her hips and knees flex involuntarily. There is no rash.
questions.q: Which is the name of the sign elicited?
questions.e: Brudzinski's sign is involuntary hip and knee flexion on passive neck flexion and indicates meningeal irritation.

steps.x: Neck flexion causing hip and knee flexion.

elim: An upgoing plantar from upper motor neurone damage.
Mastoid bruising from a basal skull fracture.
Pain or resistance on extending the knee with the hip flexed.
Electric sensation down the spine on neck flexion, seen in MS.

steps.x: C: Brudzinski's sign. Neck flex gives hip and knee flex = Brudzinski's.

questions.stem: A 26 year old nursery worker has 2 days of headache, photophobia and mild neck stiffness in August. Several children at the nursery have had a 'summer flu' with diarrhoea. She is alert. Her temperature is 38.1°C. CSF shows a lymphocytosis with normal glucose.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: Enteroviruses (echovirus, coxsackievirus) are the commonest cause of viral meningitis, spread hand-to-mouth, often after a summer flu-like illness, and are usually mild and self-limiting.

steps.x: Mild lymphocytic meningitis in summer with contact with sick children.

elim: Affects the immunocompromised with a subacute illness.
A cause of viral meningitis, but not linked to a summer nursery outbreak.
Affects neonates, elderly and immunocompromised, usually with a sicker picture.

steps.x: B: Enterovirus. Commonest viral meningitis: enterovirus.

questions.stem: A 5 month old boy is brought in with 8 hours of fever, poor feeding and drowsiness. He has a bulging fontanelle and a non-blanching petechial rash on his legs. His temperature is 39.2°C, heart rate 180 bpm and capillary refill time 4 seconds. Blood culture grows Gram-negative diplococci.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: N. meningitidis is a Gram-negative diplococcus, the commonest UK cause, peaking around 5 months and again in adolescence, with a classic non-blanching petechial rash.

steps.x: Infant with a petechial rash and Gram-negative diplococci.

elim: A Gram-negative bacillus, mainly in neonates.
Gram-positive cocci, mainly in the first weeks of life.

steps.x: D: Neisseria meningitidis. Gram-negative diplococci + rash = meningococcus.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man was treated for right lower lobe pneumonia a week ago. He now has severe headache, neck stiffness and confusion. His temperature is 39.0°C and GCS 13/15. There is no rash. CSF Gram stain shows Gram-positive diplococci.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: S. pneumoniae, a Gram-positive diplococcus, is the commonest cause of bacterial meningitis in adults, often after pneumonia or ear infection.

steps.x: Adult meningitis after pneumonia with Gram-positive diplococci.

elim: Gram-positive cocci in clusters, after neurosurgery or trauma.

steps.x: E: Streptococcus pneumoniae. Gram-positive diplococci after pneumonia/otitis = pneumococcus.

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman with rheumatoid arthritis takes prednisolone 15 mg daily and methotrexate. She has 2 days of fever, headache and confusion, and enjoys unpasteurised soft cheese from a farmers' market. Her temperature is 38.6°C. CSF Gram stain shows Gram-positive rods.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: Listeria, a Gram-positive rod, causes meningitis in neonates, the elderly and the immunocompromised, linked to unpasteurised milk and soft cheese.

steps.x: Elderly immunosuppressed woman, soft cheese, Gram-positive rods.

elim: A yeast seen with India ink, not a Gram-positive rod.

steps.x: D: Listeria monocytogenes. Gram-positive rods in the old or immunosuppressed = Listeria.

questions.stem: A 6 day old girl born at 36 weeks after prolonged rupture of membranes is lethargic, feeding poorly and has a temperature of 38.4°C. Her fontanelle is full. Her mother's vaginal swab in pregnancy was positive. CSF Gram stain shows Gram-positive cocci in chains.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: Group B Streptococcus is the commonest cause of meningitis in neonates, transmitted from maternal genital tract colonisation.

steps.x: Neonate, maternal colonisation, cocci in chains.

elim: A Gram-negative diplococcus, peaking at around 5 months.

steps.x: B: Group B Streptococcus. Neonatal meningitis: Group B Streptococcus first.

questions.stem: A 3 year old boy recently arrived in the UK and has not received any childhood vaccinations. He has 1 day of fever, irritability and neck stiffness. His temperature is 39.1°C. There is no rash. CSF Gram stain shows small Gram-negative coccobacilli.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: Haemophilus influenzae is a Gram-negative coccobacillus and causes meningitis in unvaccinated young children.

steps.x: Unvaccinated toddler with Gram-negative coccobacilli.

elim: A Gram-negative bacillus, typically in neonates.
A Gram-negative diplococcus, often with a rash.

steps.x: C: Haemophilus influenzae type b. Gram-negative coccobacilli = H. influenzae.

questions.stem: A 28 year old woman has 2 days of headache, photophobia and neck stiffness. A week ago she developed painful vesicles and ulcers on her vulva, and she has had a similar episode of meningitis before. She is alert. CSF shows a lymphocytosis with normal glucose and no organisms on Gram stain.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: HSV-2 is a recognised cause of viral meningitis, often with genital herpes and sometimes recurrent.

clues: painful vesicles and ulcers on her vulva
steps.x: Lymphocytic meningitis with genital herpes.

elim: Immunocompromised patients with a subacute illness.
The commonest viral cause, but genital ulcers point elsewhere.
Bacterial: neutrophils, low glucose and rash.

steps.x: C: Herpes simplex virus type 2. Viral meningitis + genital vesicles = HSV-2.

questions.stem: A 55 year old man had a kidney transplant 2 years ago and takes tacrolimus and mycophenolate. He has a 3 week history of worsening headache, vomiting and tiredness, and today he is drowsy. His temperature is 37.8°C. There is mild neck stiffness. CSF opening pressure is very high.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: Cryptococcal meningitis occurs in the immunocompromised with a subacute headache, vomiting and fatigue progressing to drowsiness and seizures.

steps.x: Subacute meningitis in an immunosuppressed patient.

elim: Acute and self-limiting in healthy people.
An acute illness over hours with a rash.

steps.x: A: Cryptococcus neoformans. Subacute meningitis in the immunocompromised = Cryptococcus.

questions.stem: A 17 year old girl has 6 hours of fever, leg pain and cold hands. She now has a rapidly spreading purpuric rash that does not fade under a glass. Her temperature is 39.5°C, pulse rate 138 bpm, BP 82/44 mmHg and capillary refill 5 seconds. She is alert and has no neck stiffness.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Fever, shock and a spreading non-blanching purpuric rash is meningococcal septicaemia; neck stiffness may be absent.

clues: does not fade under a glass
steps.x: Fever, shock and a spreading non-blanching rash.

elim: Not associated with shock and high fever.
Patients are well, without fever or shock.

steps.x: C: Meningococcal septicaemia. Fever + non-blanching rash + shock = meningococcal septicaemia.

questions.stem: A 20 year old university student has 2 days of headache, photophobia and mild neck stiffness following a sore throat and runny nose. He is alert, talking normally and eating. His temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 88 bpm and BP 124/78 mmHg. There is no rash or focal neurology. Investigations are shown.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A mild meningitic illness after an upper respiratory infection with lymphocytic CSF, normal glucose and no organisms is viral meningitis, which has a good prognosis.

clues: following a sore throat and runny nose
steps.x: Mild illness after a URTI with a lymphocytic CSF.

elim: Neutrophils and low glucose would be expected in a sicker patient.
Immunocompromised patients with a subacute course.
He is alert with no confusion, seizures or focal signs.
Sudden onset without a viral prodrome.

steps.x: E: Viral meningitis. Mild, post-URTI, lymphocytes, normal glucose = viral meningitis.

questions.stem: A 58 year old woman has 1 day of fever, headache and neck stiffness and is now drowsy. Her temperature is 39.2°C, pulse rate 114 bpm and GCS 13/15. CT head is normal and a lumbar puncture is performed. Investigations are shown.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Raised opening pressure, turbid CSF, high protein, a marked neutrophil pleocytosis and glucose below half the plasma level is bacterial meningitis.

steps.x: Turbid CSF, neutrophils, low glucose ratio.

elim: Subacute in the immunocompromised; India ink would be positive.

steps.x: A: Bacterial meningitis. Neutrophils + low CSF:plasma glucose = bacterial.

questions.stem: A 33 year old woman has 6 hours of headache, fever and neck stiffness. Her temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 104 bpm, BP 122/76 mmHg and GCS 15/15. There is no rash, papilloedema or focal neurology. She has no bleeding disorder. Blood cultures have been taken.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
questions.e: Lumbar puncture is the diagnostic first-line investigation, ideally before antibiotics when it can be done within 1 hour and there are no contraindications.

clues: no rash, papilloedema or focal neurology
steps.x: Suspected meningitis with no contraindication to LP.

elim: Not needed without signs of raised ICP.
Used when LP cannot be done.

steps.x: C: Lumbar puncture. No contraindication: LP, ideally before antibiotics.

questions.stem: A 15 year old boy has fever and a rapidly spreading non-blanching rash. His BP is 76/40 mmHg and capillary refill 5 seconds despite fluid boluses. He has been given IV ceftriaxone. The team want to confirm the organism.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the organism?
questions.e: When LP cannot be done, as in meningococcal septicaemia, whole blood PCR and blood cultures are used to identify N. meningitidis.

clues: He has been given IV ceftriaxone
steps.x: Septic shock with a purpuric rash: LP is unsafe.

elim: LP is contraindicated in meningococcal septicaemia.
Less useful than blood PCR after antibiotics.

steps.x: E: Whole blood meningococcal PCR. LP contraindicated: blood cultures and whole blood PCR.

questions.stem: A 49 year old man has 1 day of fever, headache and neck stiffness. His wife says he has been increasingly drowsy. His temperature is 39.0°C and GCS 11/15. Fundoscopy shows bilateral papilloedema. Blood cultures have been taken and IV ceftriaxone given.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: Signs of raised ICP (GCS under 13, papilloedema, focal deficit, new seizures) contraindicate LP, so a CT head is done first.

steps.x: Meningitis with low GCS and papilloedema.

elim: Does not address the safety of LP.
Unsafe with signs of raised ICP.

steps.x: B: CT head. Raised ICP signs: CT head before LP.

questions.stem: A 37 year old woman with suspected meningitis is about to have a lumbar puncture. She had chemotherapy for lymphoma 2 weeks ago. Her temperature is 38.7°C, BP 118/70 mmHg and GCS 15/15. There is no rash and fundoscopy is normal.
questions.q: Which feature is the strongest reason to delay the lumbar puncture until after a CT head?
questions.e: Immunocompromise is one of the features that should prompt CT head before LP, along with GCS under 13, focal deficit, new seizures, papilloedema and a known CNS lesion.

steps.x: Recent chemotherapy in suspected meningitis.

elim: A normal GCS does not contraindicate LP.
Normal fundi do not contraindicate LP.

steps.x: D: Immunocompromise. Immunocompromise: CT head before LP.

questions.stem: A 21 year old man has 2 days of headache, photophobia and neck stiffness after a week of a cold. He is alert and well perfused with no rash. His temperature is 38.0°C. CT head is normal and a lumbar puncture is performed.
questions.q: Which is the most likely CSF finding?
o: Clear fluid with lymphocytes and normal glucose
Turbid fluid with neutrophils and low glucose
questions.e: Viral meningitis gives clear or slightly turbid CSF with a lymphocytosis, negative culture, mildly raised protein and normal glucose.

clues: after a week of a cold
He is alert and well perfused
steps.x: Mild meningitis after a viral prodrome.
A: Clear fluid with lymphocytes and normal glucose. Viral CSF: clear, lymphocytes, normal glucose.

questions.stem: A 39 year old man with untreated HIV and a CD4 count of 40 cells/µL has 2 weeks of headache, vomiting and fatigue, and had a seizure today. CSF shows a raised opening pressure, raised protein and low glucose. Gram stain is negative.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate test on the CSF to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.e: Cryptococcal meningitis gives raised protein and low glucose, and India ink staining of the CSF is diagnostic.

steps.x: Advanced HIV with subacute meningitis.
C: India ink stain. Cryptococcal meningitis: India ink is diagnostic.

questions.stem: A 61 year old man with pneumococcal meningitis is on IV ceftriaxone and dexamethasone on the ward. Two hours ago his GCS was 15/15; it is now 11/15 and he is restless. His pulse rate is 58 bpm and BP 172/96 mmHg.

visual.title: Glasgow Coma Scale
visual.label: Now 11
visual.caption: GCS has fallen from 15 to 11 in 2 hours.

questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
o: Observe and repeat GCS in 4 hours
questions.e: A drop in GCS in meningitis warrants immediate ICU referral for escalating management; bradycardia and hypertension suggest raised ICP.

steps.x: Falling GCS with signs of raised ICP.
B: Immediate ICU referral. Falling GCS in meningitis: refer to ICU now.

questions.stem: A 9 year old girl is recovering from pneumococcal meningitis and is ready for discharge after 10 days of IV antibiotics. She is eating well and has had no seizures. Her parents ask which long-term problem she should be checked for before she goes home.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation before discharge?
questions.e: Sensorineural hearing loss is the commonest complication of meningitis, so all children need a formal hearing test; brain damage, seizures and death are other complications.

steps.x: Recovery from bacterial meningitis.
C: Formal audiology assessment. After meningitis: check hearing.

questions.stem: A 38 year old man sees his GP in a rural surgery with 5 hours of fever, headache, neck stiffness and a few non-blanching spots on his trunk. His temperature is 39.1°C and pulse rate 116 bpm. An ambulance has been called and will take 30 minutes. He has no allergies.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management before transfer?
o: Paracetamol and wait for the ambulance
questions.e: In primary care, suspected meningitis or meningococcal disease is treated with benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IM (or IV) before hospital transfer.

steps.x: Suspected meningococcal disease in general practice.

elim: Used for prophylaxis in contacts, not treatment.
Not given in primary care, and avoided in septicaemia.

steps.x: B: Benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IM. Primary care: benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IM, then transfer.

questions.stem: A 34 year old woman is brought to the Emergency Department with 8 hours of headache, fever, vomiting and neck stiffness. Her temperature is 39.0°C, pulse rate 112 bpm, BP 116/72 mmHg and GCS 15/15. Blood cultures have been taken and an LP cannot be done within the hour. She has no allergies.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate antibiotic?
questions.e: Adults under 60 (and children over 3 months) in A&E are treated with IV ceftriaxone, switched to IV benzylpenicillin if N. meningitidis is confirmed sensitive.

clues: cannot be done within the hour
steps.x: Suspected bacterial meningitis in an adult under 60.

elim: Used once meningococcus is confirmed sensitive.
For cephalosporin or penicillin allergy concerns.
Only added if resistant pneumococcus is suspected.

steps.x: B: IV ceftriaxone. Hospital, under 60: IV ceftriaxone without delay.

questions.stem: A 29 year old man has suspected bacterial meningitis in the Emergency Department. He had anaphylaxis with throat swelling and hypotension after a dose of cefuroxime last year. His temperature is 38.9°C and GCS 14/15. Blood cultures have been taken.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate antibiotic?
questions.e: If there is a cephalosporin or penicillin cross-reactivity concern, IV chloramphenicol is the alternative.

steps.x: Bacterial meningitis with cephalosporin anaphylaxis.

elim: A cephalosporin, which caused his anaphylaxis.
A cephalosporin, which caused his anaphylaxis.
Used for contact prophylaxis, not treatment.

steps.x: D: IV chloramphenicol. Severe beta-lactam allergy: IV chloramphenicol.

questions.stem: A 45 year old woman returned from 3 months working in Spain a week ago and finished a course of amoxicillin for sinusitis 5 days ago. She now has fever, headache and neck stiffness. CSF Gram stain shows Gram-positive diplococci. She has been started on IV ceftriaxone.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate addition to her treatment?
questions.e: IV vancomycin is added if recent travel or antibiotic use raises concern about penicillin-resistant S. pneumoniae.

steps.x: Pneumococcal meningitis with travel and recent antibiotics.
D: IV vancomycin. Resistant pneumococcus risk: add IV vancomycin.

questions.stem: A 6 week old boy is brought in with 12 hours of fever, irritability and poor feeding. His temperature is 38.7°C, heart rate 176 bpm and his fontanelle is bulging. Blood cultures have been taken and a lumbar puncture is performed.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?
questions.e: Young infants are treated with IV cefotaxime and ampicillin (or amoxicillin) to cover GBS, H. influenzae and Listeria.

steps.x: Meningitis in an infant under 3 months.

elim: Misses Listeria and is not preferred in young infants.

steps.x: B: IV cefotaxime and IV ampicillin. Under 3 months: cefotaxime plus ampicillin/amoxicillin.

questions.stem: A 76 year old man is treated empirically for bacterial meningitis. On day 2, his CSF culture grows Listeria monocytogenes sensitive to amoxicillin. He had been started on IV ceftriaxone and IV amoxicillin on admission. His renal function is normal, he has no allergies and he is improving.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate antibiotic regimen?
questions.e: Listeria is specifically treated with ampicillin plus an aminoglycoside (IV amoxicillin plus IV gentamicin); patients over 60, under 3 months or pregnant get amoxicillin cover empirically.

steps.x: Confirmed Listeria meningitis.
A: IV amoxicillin and IV gentamicin. Listeria: amoxicillin plus gentamicin.

questions.stem: A 32 year old woman who is 30 weeks pregnant has 1 day of fever, headache, photophobia and neck stiffness. Her temperature is 38.8°C, pulse rate 110 bpm and GCS 15/15. Blood cultures are taken. She has no allergies. The organism is not yet known.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?
questions.e: Patients who are pregnant, over 60 or under 3 months need Listeria cover: IV cefotaxime and IV amoxicillin.

clues: The organism is not yet known
steps.x: Bacterial meningitis in pregnancy.

elim: Misses Listeria, a risk in pregnancy.
Does not cover meningococcus well and misses Listeria.

steps.x: B: IV cefotaxime and IV amoxicillin. Pregnant: add amoxicillin for Listeria.

questions.stem: A 24 year old man has headache, photophobia and mild neck stiffness. He is alert and well. His CSF shows lymphocytes with normal glucose, the Gram stain is negative and enterovirus PCR is positive. Blood cultures at 48 hours are negative.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Viral meningitis is managed with symptomatic care: analgesia, antipyretics, nutrition and hydration.

clues: Blood cultures at 48 hours are negative
steps.x: Confirmed enteroviral meningitis.

elim: For HSV encephalitis, not enteroviral meningitis.

steps.x: A: Analgesia, antipyretics and fluids. Viral meningitis: supportive care only.

questions.stem: A 64 year old woman has fever, headache and neck stiffness. She is also disorientated, has word-finding difficulty and had a focal seizure. Her temperature is 38.9°C. CT head is normal and LP has been done. She has been given IV ceftriaxone and IV amoxicillin.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate addition while awaiting CSF results?
questions.e: Empirical antibiotics and antivirals continue until LP results are available; IV aciclovir is added when encephalitis is suspected, especially in the elderly or immunocompromised.

steps.x: Meningism plus encephalitic features.
A: IV aciclovir. Possible encephalitis: add IV aciclovir.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man has suspected pneumococcal meningitis in the Emergency Department. His temperature is 39.2°C and GCS 14/15. He has no rash and BP is 128/80 mmHg. Blood cultures are taken and IV ceftriaxone is about to be given.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate additional treatment?
questions.e: IV dexamethasone given within 4 hours of the first antibiotic dose reduces morbidity and mortality in bacterial meningitis.

clues: IV ceftriaxone is about to be given
steps.x: Bacterial meningitis without septicaemia.

elim: Not routine without signs of raised ICP.

steps.x: B: IV dexamethasone. Bacterial meningitis: add IV dexamethasone with antibiotics.

questions.stem: A 16 year old boy has fever, a spreading purpuric rash and cold peripheries. His BP is 78/42 mmHg and lactate is 6.1 mmol/L. He has no neck stiffness. He has received IV ceftriaxone and fluid boluses. A junior doctor asks whether to give dexamethasone.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate advice?
o: Do not give dexamethasone in suspected meningococcal septicaemia
Give dexamethasone 4 hours after antibiotics only
Give dexamethasone to prevent hearing loss
questions.e: Dexamethasone is contraindicated in suspected meningococcal septicaemia.

steps.x: Meningococcal septicaemia with shock.

elim: Timing is not the issue: it is contraindicated here.

steps.x: A: Do not give dexamethasone in suspected meningococcal septicaemia. No dexamethasone in meningococcal septicaemia.

questions.stem: A 7 year old girl is admitted with confirmed meningococcal meningitis. Her mother, who lives with her and has been caring for her for the past week, asks what she should do to protect herself. The mother is well and has no allergies.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management for the mother?
o: No action unless she develops symptoms
questions.e: Close contacts in the past 7 days of meningococcal disease need prophylaxis: a single dose of oral ciprofloxacin first line, with rifampicin as the alternative.

steps.x: A household contact of meningococcal disease.

elim: Treatment for suspected disease, not prophylaxis.

steps.x: E: Single dose of oral ciprofloxacin. Contacts: single-dose oral ciprofloxacin.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man has pneumococcal meningitis. On day 1 his GCS falls from 14 to 9 and he develops papilloedema. CT head shows diffuse cerebral swelling. A student asks why bacterial infection of the meninges causes the brain to swell.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism?
o: Neutrophil influx and cytokine release causing blood-brain barrier breakdown
Obstruction of venous sinuses by tumour
questions.e: Bacterial meningitis triggers an intense inflammatory response in the subarachnoid space with neutrophil influx, cytokine release and blood-brain barrier breakdown, causing cerebral oedema and raised ICP.

steps.x: Raised ICP in bacterial meningitis.

elim: Not the main cause of oedema in meningitis.

steps.x: D: Neutrophil influx and cytokine release causing blood-brain barrier breakdown. Inflammation breaks the blood-brain barrier: oedema and raised ICP.

questions.stem: A 19 year old woman with meningococcal disease has a widespread purpuric rash. Her BP is 84/50 mmHg. Her platelet count is 38 x10^9/L, INR 2.4 and fibrinogen low. Blood cultures grow Gram-negative diplococci. A student asks what causes the rash.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism?
o: Direct viral damage to the skin
questions.e: N. meningitidis endotoxin (lipooligosaccharide) drives DIC and the non-blanching purpuric rash of meningococcal septicaemia.

steps.x: Purpura with low platelets, raised INR and low fibrinogen.

elim: Does not cause a spreading purpuric rash with low fibrinogen.

steps.x: C: Endotoxin-driven disseminated intravascular coagulation. Meningococcal rash: endotoxin-driven DIC.

questions.stem: A 47 year old woman with pneumococcal meningitis is given IV dexamethasone with her first dose of IV ceftriaxone. Her daughter asks why a steroid is used when the problem is an infection, and whether it will affect her mother's hearing.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of benefit?
o: It increases antibiotic penetration into the CSF
It reduces the inflammatory response to bacterial lysis caused by antibiotics
questions.e: Dexamethasone reduces the inflammatory response to bacterial lysis triggered by antibiotics, limiting neurological damage and hearing loss.

clues: IV dexamethasone with her first dose
steps.x: A steroid given with the first antibiotic dose.

elim: Steroids reduce inflammation and may reduce penetration.
Not its role; it is avoided in septicaemia.

steps.x: D: It reduces the inflammatory response to bacterial lysis caused by antibiotics. Dexamethasone dampens the lysis-triggered inflammation.

questions.stem: A 22 year old man has viral meningitis with a CSF lymphocytosis and a CSF glucose of 3.5 mmol/L (plasma 5.4 mmol/L). His flatmate had bacterial meningitis last year with a very low CSF glucose. He asks why his glucose is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: He has a higher plasma glucose
Viruses block glucose transport into the CSF
Viruses replicate using host cell machinery without a neutrophilic response consuming glucose
questions.e: Viruses replicate inside host cells without the purulent neutrophilic response of bacterial infection, so CSF glucose is not consumed and stays normal.

steps.x: Normal CSF glucose in viral meningitis.

elim: He has viral meningitis and needs no antibiotics.

steps.x: E: Viruses replicate using host cell machinery without a neutrophilic response consuming glucose. Viral: no bacteria or neutrophils consuming glucose.
